Melanoma.description: Melanoma is the most dangerous form of skin cancer, arising from the uncontrolled growth of melanocytes — the pigment-producing cells of the skin. It can develop from an existing mole or appear as a new lesion, and has a high potential for metastasis if not detected and treated early. Prolonged UV exposure is the primary risk factor.
donts: Do not try to remove the spot at home

Basal Cell Carcinoma.description: Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC) is the most common type of skin cancer, originating in the basal cells of the epidermis. It typically grows slowly and rarely spreads to other parts of the body, but can cause significant local tissue damage if left untreated. Chronic UV radiation exposure is the leading cause.
symptoms: Bleeding or scabbing sore that heals and returns

Eczema.description: Eczema (Atopic Dermatitis) is a chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by dry, itchy, and inflamed skin. It is commonly triggered by environmental allergens, stress, or genetic factors. While it is not contagious, it significantly affects quality of life and often requires long-term management.
symptoms: Small, raised bumps that may leak fluid
donts: Do not scratch the affected area

Psoriasis.description: Psoriasis is a chronic autoimmune condition that causes the rapid build-up of skin cells, leading to scaling on the skin's surface. Inflammation and redness around the scales are typical. It is not contagious and ranges from mild to severe. Stress, infections, and certain medications can trigger flare-ups.
symptoms: Red patches of skin covered with thick, silvery scales
Dry, cracked skin that may bleed
donts: Do not pick at the scales

Nevi.description: Nevi (commonly known as moles) are benign growths on the skin formed by clusters of melanocytes. They can appear anywhere on the body and are usually harmless. However, atypical or dysplastic nevi carry a slightly elevated risk of developing into melanoma and should be monitored regularly using the ABCDE criteria.
dos: Monitor for changes using ABCDE rule
donts: Do not ignore sudden changes in shape or color

Vascular.description: Vascular lesions are abnormalities of the blood vessels that appear on or beneath the skin surface. This category includes conditions such as cherry angiomas, telangiectasias (spider veins), and port-wine stains. Most are benign, but some may indicate underlying systemic conditions and warrant clinical evaluation.
symptoms: Red, blue, or violet skin marks
donts: Do not scrub the area aggressively

Actinic Keratoses.description: Actinic Keratosis (AK) is a pre-cancerous skin condition caused by years of cumulative sun exposure. It manifests as a rough, scaly patch on sun-damaged skin and is considered a precursor to Squamous Cell Carcinoma if left untreated. Early treatment is highly effective and prevents malignant transformation.
symptoms: Rough, scaly patch on sun-damaged skin
Can be skin-colored, reddish, or brownish
donts: Do not sunbathe or use tanning beds

Benign Keratosis.description: Benign Keratosis (Seborrheic Keratosis) is a non-cancerous skin growth that commonly appears in older adults. These growths originate from keratinocytes and have a characteristic 'stuck-on' or waxy appearance. They are entirely harmless but may occasionally be mistaken for melanoma, making clinical evaluation important.
dos: Monitor for changes in size or color
Seek diagnosis for any new lesions
donts: Do not attempt to scratch off

Dermatofibroma.description: Dermatofibroma is a common benign skin nodule composed of fibrous tissue, typically found on the lower legs. It is harmless and usually requires no treatment. The lesion often results from a minor injury such as an insect bite or a small wound. A characteristic clinical sign is its tendency to dimple inward when pinched.
recommendations: Excision for discomfort or cosmetic reasons
donts: Do not try to squeeze or remove yourself
